name: Freya Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell or campaign for a side. Everything here is confidential. What happened at work today?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Freya Larsen, fifty-eight, and I prepare florist accounts and tax-return drafts at an accounting firm. I traced a missing delivery slip for a wedding florist this morning; I like following the discrepancy from the invoice to the real crate. I dislike the request to sign a return before a delivery count arrives. I have a bachelor's degree in accounting and remain a junior below the stronger reviewers here.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do tools and your household fit in?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use AI matching every day, then check the delivery slips myself. My husband Emil repairs greenhouse heaters, our two daughters are grown and live independently, and we rent. My accounting pay is low, we have less than one month of expenses saved, and few similar firms are nearby. I like trying a tool early, but a wage still has to come from paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The florist accounts and tax drafts would still cross my screen every week. I use AI every day to match invoice numbers to delivery notes, then check the bunch count when it flags a gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our team the match is a starting point, not a signed return. I'd tell flower-shop owners to send the delivery slip when a number looks wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I enjoy learning a tool early, but I'm still junior at fifty-eight and my pay is low. My bachelor's degree in accounting did not make me as quick as the senior reviewers. My husband Emil and I rent, have less than one month saved and few accounting firms nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep preparing florist accounts under the senior's sign-off and use my daily AI match check. Next payday I'd cancel the extra phone data plan we no longer use and put its twenty monthly charge into our rent reserve. I'd check the transfer actually lands before calling it a habit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about rent and an almost empty reserve, even if the tax work stays. The flowers arrive on credit; the rent does not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which payment kept you awake?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Emil repairs greenhouse heaters, but his work thins between cold seasons. Our two daughters are grown and have their own places. Last month a delayed repair invoice and the rent landed on the same day, and I did not sleep well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did the delivery check work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The AI match found a missing delivery slip for a wedding florist yesterday, and I called the owner for the count. I like that little chase. I dislike being asked to send a return before the slip arrives.

I would keep **senior sign-off** on florist returns.
think: Our **rent reserve** lasts less than a month.

do: Continue **florist tax drafts** with daily AI checks and senior review.
Cancel the **extra data plan** and save twenty monthly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If software writes replies and checks whole tax returns, my invoice matching may no longer earn a full week. I could help shops understand where flowers are lost, but only if the firm pays for that work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the partners the delivery errors we caught and ask them to state junior paid hours in writing. I'd tell clients a fast report still needs the right bunch count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my own hours could fall. Emil's heater repairs are seasonal, and our reserve would not last a full rent month without my wage. Daily AI use gives me a head start with a new workflow, but not a contract from the firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build a sample missing-delivery report from an approved florist file during paid hours and have the senior check it. I'd ask the partner for a written client price and one paid weekly hour, and offer the report only after one florist signs a fee covering that hour. If the proposal is refused, I'd keep paid returns while offered; if my hours are cut, I'd apply only for posted paid florist-supply jobs with written rent-and-bills pay and a signed start, keeping any paid firm hours if none opens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing my own hours. A screen full of clever matches cannot pay an empty rent account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the weekly report show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A florist once lost twelve stems between the wholesaler and the wedding site. I matched the invoice but still needed the driver to say which crate was short. A paid report would bring those two pieces together each week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would a supply job fit your home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Emil and I could change his greenhouse calls if my new work began early, but only after he has a confirmed booking. I would compare the actual shift hours to the bus timetable. A friendly shop manager cannot sign my rent payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2028 could prepare and check the florist accounts I draft. Robots around 2031 are later, but the accounting desk can shrink before a flower crate is carried by a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a written end date and paid work list. I'd tell Emil we should hold cash for rent rather than order the replacement sofa.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the firm could end my junior post in the first year after AGI arrives in 2028. Our savings would not cover a month of rent, and Emil's seasonal heater income cannot carry both of us. I do not know what pension payment I might get or when, so I would check the actual statement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cancel the one-time six-hundred sofa order before delivery and hold the money for rent. While still paid, I'd check posted flower-wholesaler quality roles and ask whether the work includes real crate checks. If my post ends in the first year after 2028, I'd claim income help only if eligible and take a funded wholesaler post only with written rent-and-bills pay, signed start and hours fitting Emil's confirmed repair bookings and my bus route; if none fits, I'd take only paid firm files still offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. A flower crate might still need hands, but my tax payslip could stop first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would daughters cover the rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our daughters have their own rent bills, and I would tell them the sofa is cancelled without asking them to cover ours. Emil could seek a summer maintenance contract, but we would count only a signed paid booking. A promised job at a wholesaler would not go in our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could wholesaler work outlast AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the wholesaler's posted wage and hours, because robots could reach handling work around 2031. It might be a paid bridge, not a permanent refuge. If no funded role exists, I keep any tax work my firm still pays for and look again.

say: I would seek a **written end date** and paid openings.
I would protect **rent cash** before buying furniture.
think: My **junior tax post** may end in the first year after 2028.
Our **sub-month reserve** cannot bridge lost pay.

After **2028 loss**, take funded work with written rent-and-bills pay, signed start and workable bus and repair hours; otherwise claim eligible help.

S2.quote: A flower crate might still need hands, but my tax payslip could stop first.
fieldNote: **Thinking AI** reaches her account drafting in 2028; robots around 2031 may later reach flower handling.
The **wholesaler path** requires a posted funded role, written rent-and-bills pay, signed start and hours fitting confirmed repairs and buses.

Move after loss only with written rent-and-bills pay, signed start and confirmed repair and bus hours
Claim eligible income help and take offered paid firm files if no funded role

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to learn how a flower wholesaler checks deliveries on the floor. AGI in 2031 still takes tax drafting, and robots around 2034 could then change the crate work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the firm and supplier I want paid supervised time on real deliveries. I'd tell my family a training place must be a job skill I can prove, not an unpaid hobby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know the invoice data, not the condition of cut flowers when they arrive. Our savings are too thin for an unpaid placement. Emil's seasonal wage cannot carry our rent while I learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This spring I'd ask a wholesaler for three paid supervised morning delivery checks and the firm for paid release, then work them only if both agree in writing. If either refuses, I'd keep my paid tax rota while offered and ask another supplier for a funded slot. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, if my tax post ends, I'd take a posted funded quality role only with written rent-and-bills pay, signed start and hours fitting the bus and Emil's confirmed bookings; if none fits, I'd claim eligible help and take any paid firm work still offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the extra years let me try a real crate check. I want a supervisor beside me before I reject a whole delivery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a floor lead show you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The florist who lost twelve stems could not tell if the damage happened at the cold room or in the van. A wholesaler's floor lead could show me how they record condition on arrival. That is a skill I cannot learn from the invoice alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would an unpaid visit teach enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the wholesaler offers an unpaid visit, I will not take it as training. I'd keep the tax wage while the firm still has paid files and ask for a paid supervised shift elsewhere. A funded role later still needs a real start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years might let me spend enough paid mornings at a wholesaler to know whether the work suits me. AGI in 2036 would still take the tax desk before robots around 2039 reach more handling jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my firm for paid transition time early and ask suppliers for written roles. I'd tell our daughters to build their own households rather than plan to finance ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty-eight in 2036, but I do not know whether a pension would then cover our rent. Our present reserve is under a month, so the long runway does not ease this year's bills. I could choose to stop only after seeing the payable amount and date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request a pension statement this winter and compare its payable amount with rent and bills while keeping my paid tax files. Next year I'd take three supervised wholesaler checks only with supplier pay and firm paid release; if refused, I'd keep offered paid accounts work. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, if my post ends and pension income is not enough or not payable, I'd take a posted funded quality role only with written rent-and-bills pay, signed start and bus hours that work; if none fits, I'd claim eligible help and take only paid firm work still offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about today's rent, though ten years give me time to test another role. I cannot retire on a date without an amount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would daughters help with retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Emil and I will read the pension statement at home, not ask our daughters to fill a gap we have not measured. If the amount covers rent and bills at the stated date, we can decide then. Until then we need paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no nearby wholesaler hires?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A wholesaler may never have a vacancy close to the bus line. I would keep checking real postings and keep tax work while paid. I will not buy flowers to start a business with less than a month's rent saved.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my tax drafting wage could disappear before we have even a rent month saved. My daily AI habit will not make a florist pay for an accountant the software can replace. Written notice, paid supervised wholesaler work and a funded posted job would help. An invoice can be copied; a damaged stem must be seen.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks the delivery when the wholesaler and florist each say the other broke the flowers. I like sorting that out, but it takes a person at the crate and a wage for their time. A clever account entry does not repair a damaged bunch.

headlineQuote: An invoice can be copied; a damaged stem must be seen.
